The hit tool is real, but without secondary skills or early power development, the path to impact is narrow.

829058_hitter.text: Gabriel Davalillo is an 18-year-old third baseman showing mixed bat discipline and pop: he's posting .267/.348/.410 with an 11% walk rate and .143 ISO over 227 A-ball plate appearances, though both his strikeout rate (25.6%) and isolated power rank near the middle of the minor-league field. The real concern is that his average and slugging power lag below the tools expected at the position—his .267 AVG is strong for his age, but ISO in the 47th percentile signals he hasn't yet connected the bat to game power. The sample is current and meaningful, but at 18 with moderate command and modest thump so far, this looks like a years-away organizational depth profile rather than a near-term contributor.

829210_hitter.text: Ty Harvey is a 19-year-old catcher showing early discipline at the plate—19% BB% on a 58 PA sample—but swinging and missing at a concerning clip (24.1% K%). His .107 ISO translates to below-average raw power for a catcher, and the strikeout rate (24.1%), even accounting for youth, sits above league average in the MLB equivalent read. The sample is small and fresh, so expect volatility as he faces stiffer velocity and sequencing.

829854_hitter.text: Luis Arana is an 18-year-old A-level shortstop who commands the strike zone exceptionally—posting 19.2% BB% over 78 PA—but whose overall bat lacks impact, evidenced by a modest .127 ISO and a .460 SLG despite the strong .462 OBP. The approach grade is elite relative to his peer group; the hit tool is solid; but power and overall impact are well below average, and that power ceiling is the central constraint. At 78 plate appearances in a current season sample, confidence in the profile is limited, though the plate discipline suggests a repeatable skill.

830239_hitter.text: The ISO is the argument: .243 at A+ over 331 plate appearances, which translates to .159 at the MLB level, right at league average for raw power despite coming from a 22-year-old center fielder. The .885 OPS and 15 home runs alongside 18 stolen bases make the impact grade look earned, not fluky. What complicates it is the 27% strikeout rate, because that translates to 29.5% against big-league pitching, and a hit tool that grades 55 can carry a 27% K-rate in the minors long before it can carry one against advanced arms. If the contact holds, Walton profiles as a low-end everyday regular with speed-and-power upside; if pitchers find the hole, what's left is a bench bat with real pop.

830336_pitcher.text: A 1.4 ERA and 0.80 WHIP at Low-A are the kind of numbers that make you squint, but the K-BB% of 32 is the detail that earns a second look. Peters is missing bats at a 12.7 K/9 while walking fewer than two per nine, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his walk rate below the league-average 3.2, which is the part that travels. The ceiling here is a setup or multi-inning arm, not a rotation piece, and the risk is that a lefty doing this damage in A-ball still has two to three years of translation left to prove.

830402_pitcher.text: Kendry Chourio is an 18-year-old command artist who doesn't miss bats — and at A/A+, that's a profile worth understanding clearly before you fall in love with the ERA. The 2.5 ERA and 0.9 WHIP are real; his BB/9 of 1.7 and WHIP sit at the 98th and 97th percentiles respectively against his pitcher pool, and a K-BB% of 20% shows he's not walking people into trouble. The problem is the strikeout rate — 8.9 K/9 in A-ball translates to a projected 7.2 at the MLB level, below the 8.6 average, and the miss grade here is a 35 — so the question isn't whether his command is special, it's whether there's enough swing-and-miss to survive as he climbs. ValuCast projects a useful MLB arm as the most likely outcome, with the ceiling a depth arm and a multi-inning floor, and he's ticking up slightly in ValuCast's rankings over the last three days — but the outcome here lives or dies on whether the strikeout tool develops.

832562_pitcher.text: The strikeout rate is loud — 12.9 K/9 at A/A+ levels, sitting at the 90th percentile among this pitcher pool, with a K-BB% that grades 92nd. The translation to MLB context is where the profile gets honest: the whiffs carry over near league average, but the 4.2 BB/9 becomes a 4.3 in MLB equivalent terms, and walks are already the gap between a useful arm and a depth arm. Command graded at 50 by the projection, run prevention at 45, which means the upside here is a pitcher who strikes people out and lives with walks rather than one who sequences his way through lineups. If the command tightens even modestly, the bat-missing shape across 60.6 IP is believable enough to push him toward the useful MLB arm outcome the projection puts at 85%; if it doesn't, he's a multi-inning reliever who runs deep counts and eats innings without eating hitters.

834962_hitter.text: The .222 ISO across 336 PA is doing real work here, and at 23 it's showing up against legitimate arms. DePino is slashing .276/.387/.498 through AA and A+ this year, with the translated walk rate landing at 10.2%, comfortably above the big-league mean, which tells you the .387 OBP isn't just a BABIP mirage. The knock is the translation: that ISO compresses to .157 at the MLB level, right around average, so the profile hinges on whether the hit tool against upper-minors breaking stuff holds up when the sample doubles in tougher competition. If it does, you've got a first baseman who earns everyday at-bats; if the strikeout rate creeps past that translated 23.1%, the floor is a reserve corner bat who provides depth and nothing more.

834978_pitcher.text: Danny Thompson Jr. is a right-handed pitcher showing plus strikeout stuff paired with walk management that trails his miss rate—a profile built on swing-and-miss with control that lags behind the swing-and-miss. In his A+ sample (47.3 IP), he struck out 12.93 per 9 while walking 4.56 per 9, a K-BB% of 21.9% that ranks 91st percentile among ValuCast's pitcher pool. The core risk is whether he can sustain that strikeout rate as competition tightens; his current AA sample is only 9 IP, making any read here thin and provisional. Floor is a depth arm, with modest probability of reaching useful depth relief value in the next one to two years.
